learningObjective: Compare AOT artifact deployment (all lowering done ahead of first invocation) with JIT compilation (lowering triggered on the first suitable call), and identify the trade-offs.

canonicalClaims.claim: AOT compilation produces a deployable artifact whose lowering is complete before run time, avoiding first-call warmup and removing the compiler from the deployment surface; the trade-off is that shape/dtype/hardware assumptions are baked in at build time. JIT compiles lazily on first call, offering shape flexibility at the cost of first-call latency and a compiler dependency at run time.
conditions: Both stacks emit comparable kernels, so we are contrasting compilation phase not codegen quality.
Deployment target has a well-defined hardware/driver profile.
nonImplications: Does not imply AOT cannot support dynamic shapes; some stacks support ranges or optimization profiles.
Does not imply JIT re-optimizes on every call; JIT typically caches compiled artifacts per (shape, dtype, device) key.

misconceptions.claim: JIT is always faster at steady state because it can re-optimize per call.
misconceptions.whyWrong: JIT does not re-optimize per call; it caches artifacts. At steady state an AOT artifact is typically no slower than the JIT cache hit.

misconceptions.claim: AOT and JIT are indistinguishable in production.
misconceptions.whyWrong: AOT decouples the compiler from the runtime dependency; JIT requires the compiler at deployment.

misconceptions.claim: AOT requires the source model at run time.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The whole point of AOT is that the runtime only needs the emitted artifact, not the source.

misconceptions.claim: AOT is incompatible with dynamic shapes.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Modern AOT stacks (AOTInductor dynamic dims, TensorRT optimization profiles) support shape ranges within predeclared bounds.
